Arbelos PWW

GeometryCirclesArea
Game: A curved knife shape sits between three half-circles, and a circle on the upright line has just as much room inside it.
How to play: Drag the dot along the bottom line, or focus it and press the arrow keys. Press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Move the dot and the knife changes shape, yet the circle standing on the upright changes with it. The two always have exactly the same area. The picture is a proof without words: it uses Euclid's favourite proof of the Pythagorean theorem three times.

A half-circle on a side of a right triangle

Euclid did not compare squares on the sides: he drew similar shapes on them. A semicircle with diameter d has area πd²/8, so its area grows like the square of its diameter. For a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is the sum of the squares of the two legs. Therefore the semicircle on the hypotenuse equals the two semicircles on the legs put together.

semicircle(AB) = semicircle(AD) + semicircle(BD)

The upright DN is perpendicular to AB, and D sits on the big circle, so triangle ADB is right-angled at D by Thales' theorem.

Blue and red, two more times

Now look at the smaller right triangles AND and BND. Each has the upright as one leg, and each gives another Euclid step:

blue: semicircle(AD) = semicircle(AN) + semicircle(ND)
red: semicircle(BD) = semicircle(BN) + semicircle(ND)

Those are the two smaller blue and red half-circles. The biggest blue one is on AD and the biggest red one is on BD, matching the page's description.

The knife and the circle

Putting all three lines together cancels the two sloping semicircles:

big − small left − small right = semicircle(ND) + semicircle(ND)

Two equal half-circles on DN make one whole circle. The left side is the arbelos; the right side is the circle on the upright. Write AN = a and NB = b. The upright is their geometric mean, h = √(a×b), so both areas are πa×b/4. This is Archimedes' Proposition 4, and the logic test checks it at thousands of positions.

About the original

The Java applet used pink for the big half-circle, blue and red for the small ones, an orange circle standing on the upright and grey guide lines; the same parts appear here in the site's colours. Its internal "about" text was a leftover from a polygon applet and said nothing about this figure. The applet also rounded the upright to a whole pixel before drawing, while the picture here keeps the exact length; that changes nothing about the proof.

Press N in the middle, then drag the dot close to A. The knife and its circle shrink together, but the two numbers in the status line stay equal.
